idiom_name: WPF Application.Windows registry + shell ContentControl with per-view-model DataTemplates
implementation_notes: WPF provides both halves: Application.Current.Windows is the collection of instantiated Window objects and Window.Show/Activate/Close are the open/switch/dispose commands, while a shell view model that exposes a CurrentViewModel property bound to a ContentControl (with one DataTemplate per view-model type) takes the place of the classic view registry, because switching the view model switches the visual tree. Lifetime stays the handler's job: windows are removed from the collection when they are closed, and a view model must never hold the Window it is displayed in, or the view outlives its screen. What remains the application's responsibility is the decision half of change propagation - which view model observes which part of the model and when to re-query - because binding keeps views in sync with their view model but does not create the handler's dependency knowledge.
pitfalls: Application.Current.Windows holds strong references to instantiated windows: a window the shell or a view model also references keeps its data alive until Close, so registries of views must be cleared in the Closed handler.
A view model must not hold a Window or control reference; binding and commands are the only channel, otherwise the view's lifetime is extended past its window and the DataTemplate cannot recreate it.

Switching a ContentControl's content discards the previous view's visual tree and any UI state that was not in the view model (scroll position, focus, selection) - keep that state in the view model or keep both views alive in a TabControl/ItemsControl.
UI objects are thread-affine: a model change raised on a background thread must be marshalled with Dispatcher.Invoke/InvokeAsync before the registry or the views are touched.
